text: Stay awake for just one night, and your brain starts acting as if you had been drinking.
Keep going, and your whole body begins to struggle.
So what really happens when you don't sleep?
First, how much sleep do we need?
Health agencies say most adults need at least seven hours a night.
Yet in the United States, about one adult in three regularly gets less.
Now let's follow the clock.
Hour eighteen. Your reactions slow down and your attention drifts.
According to the CDC, being awake this long affects you about as much as a blood alcohol level of zero point zero five percent.
Hour twenty-four. That effect climbs to about zero point one zero percent.
That is above the legal limit for driving in the United States.
Your brain also starts taking microsleeps: blackouts of a few seconds, often without you noticing.
Why does the brain suffer so fast? Because sleep is not just rest.
In studies on mice, scientists saw fluid flowing through the brain during sleep, washing away waste.
Skip sleep, and that cleaning shift is cut short.
Sleep is also when your brain sorts and stores what you learned during the day.
Without it, new memories form less well, and focusing becomes much harder.
Your body chemistry changes too.
Several studies show that short sleep shifts two hunger hormones.
Ghrelin, which makes you hungry, goes up. Leptin, which tells you you're full, goes down.
No wonder you crave snacks after a bad night.
Your emotions get louder.
Research suggests that the amygdala, the brain's alarm center, overreacts after a sleepless night.
Small problems suddenly feel much bigger.
And after several days?
In nineteen sixty-four, a seventeen-year-old student named Randy Gardner stayed awake for about eleven days.
Toward the end, he struggled to speak, to remember and to focus, and he saw things that were not there.
Then he slept, and recovered.
For most of us, the real danger is not one dramatic all-nighter.
It is short sleep, night after night.
Health agencies link it to a higher risk of heart disease, type two diabetes, obesity and depression.
Sleep is not lost time. It is your body's nightly maintenance.
